lead: An RF passive part stores or converts energy without gain: an inductor stores magnetic energy, a capacitor stores electric energy, and a varactor is a capacitor tuned by voltage. At radio frequency the same part also has resistance, stray capacitance and stray inductance. These parasitics set loss, matching and tuning range. Every receiver front end, filter and voltage-controlled oscillator uses them. The quality factor Q is 2π times stored energy divided by energy lost per cycle; high Q means low loss and narrow resonance.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for microstrip and transmission-line parasitics, and Unit 4 for microwave integrated circuits and MMIC passives.

blocks.text: An on-chip inductor is usually a spiral of metal. The spiral creates magnetic flux and gives inductance L in henry. The same metal has series resistance R<sub>s</sub> in ohm. The turns also have capacitance to each other and to the substrate; call it shunt capacitance C<sub>p</sub> in farad. At low frequency the part looks like L in series with R<sub>s</sub>. At higher frequency C<sub>p</sub> takes current, so the impedance is no longer a pure inductor.

blocks.where: f<sub>SR</sub> is self-resonant frequency in Hz; L is inductance in H; C<sub>p</sub> is shunt capacitance in F.

blocks.text: Below f<sub>SR</sub> the part is inductive; above it the part is capacitive. The quality factor at a frequency where C<sub>p</sub> is small is:

blocks.where: ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s; L is inductance in H; R<sub>s</sub> is series resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: Skin effect pushes current to the metal surface as f rises, so R<sub>s</sub> grows roughly with √f. Eddy currents in the substrate add more loss. A typical on-chip spiral has Q in the single digits to low tens and takes much chip area. The design trade is simple: wider metal lowers R<sub>s</sub> but raises C<sub>p</sub> and lowers f<sub>SR</sub>.

An RF capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. A MIM capacitor uses two metal layers with a thin insulator between them. A MOS capacitor uses the gate oxide of a transistor. MIM capacitors are linear and have low series resistance, so they suit filters and matching networks. MOS capacitors are free in a CMOS process but their capacitance changes with gate voltage.
Both have series resistance R<sub>s</sub> in the plates and vias. They also have series inductance L<sub>s</sub> from the connecting metal. At low frequency the quality factor is:

blocks.where: C is capacitance in F; R<sub>s</sub> is series resistance in Ω; ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: Series L<sub>s</sub> causes a self-resonance, just as shunt C<sub>p</sub> does for an inductor. Above that frequency the capacitor looks inductive. A MIM capacitor usually has higher Q and tighter tolerance; a MOS capacitor saves area and can be tuned. Layout decides which parasitics dominate: short, wide connections lower R<sub>s</sub> and L<sub>s</sub> but add capacitance to nearby metal. MMIC passives are covered in Unit 4.

A varactor is a voltage-variable capacitor. Some syllabi call it a voltage-variable capacitor. A diode varactor is a reverse-biased p-n junction. Reverse bias widens the depletion region, so capacitance falls. A MOS varactor uses the gate capacitance of a MOS device, which also changes with gate voltage. Write the capacitance as C(V). The tuning range is C<sub>max</sub> / C<sub>min</sub>, the ratio at the two bias limits. A large ratio gives a wide tuning band; a small ratio gives fine control.

blocks.where: C(V) is the voltage-dependent capacitance in F; R<sub>s</sub> is series resistance in Ω; ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: Rs is the series resistance of the diode or the gate and channel. Q falls when C is large and when Rs is large. In a voltage-controlled oscillator, the varactor is part of the resonant tank. Any noise on the control voltage changes C(V), which changes frequency; this becomes phase noise. The bias line therefore needs filtering and a clean reference. Diode varactors often give a wide range; MOS varactors suit CMOS integration. The tuning range, Q and control-line noise trade against each other. See oscillators and phase noise.

figure.caption: The tree groups the three passive families and puts the worked-example values on the inductor and capacitor branches. Notice that Q and self-resonance are separate limits: the inductor works at 2 GHz only because that is below its 3.56 GHz self-resonance.

spec.aria: RF passives split into inductor, capacitor and varactor, with the worked-example values and the voltage-tuned varactor highlighted.

examples.question: A 2 nH on-chip spiral inductor at 2 GHz has series resistance 4 Ω and shunt capacitance 1 pF. Find its quality factor Q, its equivalent parallel resistance R_p using R_p ≈ Q² R_s, and its self-resonant frequency f_SR. State whether 2 GHz is below self-resonance.
steps: 2×10⁹ Hz < 3.56×10⁹ Hz, so 2 GHz is below self-resonance.
examples.answer: Q = 6.28, R_p ≈ 157.9 Ω, and f_SR ≈ 3.56 GHz; 2 GHz is below self-resonance.
examples.check:
import math
L = 2e-9
f = 2e9
R = 4.0
Cp = 1e-12
w = 2*math.pi*f
Q = w*L/R
Rp = Q**2*R
f0 = 1/(2*math.pi*math.sqrt(L*Cp))
print(round(Q,2))
print(round(Rp,1))
print(round(f0/1e9,2))

traps: Using C = 1/(2πfX) for a real capacitor above self-resonance; the part may be inductive.
Quoting one Q over a wide band; Q depends on frequency through R_s, skin effect and C(V).
Swapping the Q formulas: inductor Q = ωL/R_s, capacitor Q = 1/(ω C R_s).
Ignoring varactor bias-line noise; a clean DC control is part of the RF design.
Confusing tuning range C_max/C_min with Q; a wide range can still have low Q.

quiz.q: Define quality factor Q of an inductor and give its low-frequency formula.
quiz.a: Q is 2π times stored energy divided by energy lost per cycle; for a series inductor Q = ωL/R_s.

quiz.q: Why does an on-chip spiral stop behaving as an inductor above f_SR?
quiz.a: Shunt capacitance resonates with L; above f_SR the capacitive current dominates and impedance becomes capacitive.

quiz.q: A capacitor has C = 2 pF and series R_s = 5 Ω at 1 GHz. Find Q.
A VCO uses a varactor with noisy bias. Explain how bias noise becomes phase noise.
quiz.a: Bias noise changes C(V), shifts tank resonance, and modulates frequency; this frequency modulation appears as phase noise around the carrier.

quiz.q: Why is a MIM capacitor often preferred over a MOS capacitor in a filter?
quiz.a: MIM is linear, has higher Q and tighter tolerance; MOS capacitance varies with voltage and has more loss.

quiz.q: An inductor has L = 1 nH and R_s = 2 Ω at 5 GHz. Find Q and say if raising L to 2 nH with the same R_s doubles Q.
quiz.a: ω = 2π × 5×10⁹ = 3.142×10¹⁰ rad/s. Q = ωL/R_s = (3.142×10¹⁰ × 1×10⁻⁹)/2 = 15.7. With same R_s, 2 nH gives 31.4, but real larger L raises R_s and C_p, so Q does not exactly double.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, RF passives move into the package and onto silicon: 3D inductors, metal-oxide-metal capacitors, and digitally switched capacitor banks. Varactors are used in tunable filters, phase shifters and frequency synthesizers. Researchers study how layout, temperature and aging shift C(V) and Q. Search for RF CMOS passives, varactor linearity and on-chip inductor self-resonance to go deeper.
